#15111 1 2007-05-05T11:00:41Z southpaw
Alright, I guess you could call me a noob, but whatever. I have decided to make an entire episode of N levels, but since I have work that needs to be done I am not going to get the levels finished. This is where you come in.

Anybody who wants to join can go ahead and make a map.

Anybody who wants to judge PM me. 5 judges max including me, first come first serve.

Here are the rules and procedures:

1. Think of your favorite show. Imagine your favorite episode inside your head. If the show is funny then start laughing. If its sad, then start crying, unless you are in a public setting. If your emo, then go ahead and cry.

2. Now, take your favorite show and incorporate it into a N map. It can be from any show, although more popular shows would get more attention from the general public than not popular shows. The first map in this episode is from "Dr. Who," which is the longest running TV series.

3. I'm looking for 4 maps. The 4 maps with the highest scores by the end of the contest will be included.

4. Each contestant may submit only three maps each and each map must be playable. DDA's allowed, and KRADDA's are encouraged. If you can create a playable, difficult level out of N Art or tileset, then be my guest.

5. Judges may submit their own maps, but they cannot judge their own maps. The judging will be out of 40 points as follows:
a.) Gameplay - 15 points total
b.) Relevance to chosen show - 10 points
c.) Difficulty - 10 points
d.) Style - 5 points
If there happens to be a tie anywhere between 1st place and 3rd place, the judges will vote on which map is the weakest link.


To get full points on difficulty, make a map that isn't too hard and isn't too easy. I figure if someone dies about 10 to 15 times before they figure out and beat the map, then that is probably good for difficulty.

Style is pretty much free points, so long as you choose one or two styles, such as DDA, Puzzle, Action, etc.


This contest ends on May 30th, so get started! I basically just joined Metanet today, although I've been playing N for a while. Submit maps to NUMA (obviously) and put in the description, "For the Favorite Show episode contest." PM a link to your map to me and I will send it to the judges for judging.

That is pretty much it. If you have any questions then go ahead and ask. Yes, this is a nerd contest. No, there are no prizes, but you may generate a somewhat larger fan base. Plus, this is an entire episode, which makes it more meaningful I think.

Looking forward to seeing your creations,
321southpaw



Judging Slots:
1. ZeroTruths
2. Animator

#15462 1 2007-05-31T18:39:43Z southpaw
I will edit this later when I have more time, but although I will be busy with the Sig Tag contest I thought it would be really cool to create you own contest for N. I think there are a lot of good ideas out there that don't get put into action and if Metanet created their own contest I think that would be something really interesting.

It's sort of like a contest within a contest.


Please make your contest relating to N considering it's already in the N forum and I dont want to request a move...

The way this will work is by nominating an idea. I think 2 ideas per person would be good, and from there a poll will be taken for users to vote on their favorite idea. There will most likely be multiple polls if the number of ideas goes over 10, since you can only have 10 answers per poll.

If there are multiple polls then the winners from each poll will be polled against each other. From there the rules are formulated.


The first round will start out by nominating a certain type of contest - ie a prisoner contest, a swiss contest, etc etc (please be more original than these). PM me your nomination idea with a brief explanation of why you think your idea would be different.

The second round will consist of the rules of the contest, allowing users to really make their own contest here. We will start off with rule 1, with each person submitting two ideas for rule one. Then we move on to rule 2, etc, until we decide there are enough rules. You may submit your same submissions from Rule 1 to Rule 2 and any subsequent rounds, so long as they are not already part of the rules.

Once the rules have been decided on you will submit judging criteria, ie what should be judged and what shouldn't. To start I would ask that each person submit only one choice, but if need be I will grant two submissions.

Then we will nominate prizes, although I may just ask you to come up with the prizes you want.


And although people may say that this should be in messageboard games... well, it is a contest to create an N contest so I think there is some merit of it being here. Plus this post was up for grabs.

tell me what you think.

Are you ready to find out who the best sig tagger is on metanet?

Sig tags come in all shapes and sizes...

The Rules:


1. There are no particular rules besides the ones stated below. Create your sickest sig tag and then post it in the forum. Judging will take place from there.

2. There are three categories:

i. sigatar set
ii. small sig tag
iii. large sig tag (aka signature)

Users may enter 3 submissions for each category. Judging criteria down below.

3. Contestants may only submit 3 sigs total. You may not submit 3 sigs for each category, but you are welcome to submit two sigs to one category. Please include a title so that judges can differentiate your sigs easier.

4. Anybody may submit sig tags between June 10th and July 31st. All sig tags must be ones that have been created during this contest. Sig tags can be cropped, or just pictures with a cool background, but make them however you want.

Judging:
There will be 5 judging slots, plus a sixth so that judges can submit their own sig tags and not have to rate their own. I don't know how long it takes to make an INCREDIBLE sig tag, but I figure within the next 6 weeks is good.

Contestants are invited to bribe others to vote for them. BRIBES MUST BE DONE VIA PM. ANY BRIBES FOUND POSTED IN THIS FORUM WILL RESULT IN DISQUALIFICATION.

Non-contestants are invited to campaign for their favorite. CAMPAIGNING MAY BE DONE IN THE FORUMS AND WILL NOT RESULT IN DISQUALIFICATION OF YOUR FAVORITE.


The Categories!:

Sigatar set
Design (Is the design impressive?) - X/10
Theme (is there a central idea?) - X/5
Flow (Does everything fit together?) - X/10
Avatar (Does the avatar go with the sig?) - X/5 <---Free points pretty much
Overall look - X/20
---
Total X/50


Small sig tag
Colors (how well the colors work together) - X/10
Theme - X/10
Flow - X/10
Overall look - X/20
---
Total X/50


Large sig tag
Colors - X/15
Theme - X/5
Design - X/15
Overall look - X/15
---
Total X/50


Judges should PM me the rating for each sig tag but posting directly in the forum is alright too.

-----

PRIZES:

1. DEDICATION map and, well... a little sig tag saying you won this contest, plus immense bragging rights.
2. DED map and sig tag saying you won second
3. sig tag saying you won third.

Judging slots:

2. Spawn of Yanni

So yeah, if I were trapped in the woods with my iPhone, I would be sure to bring along my iPod too, just so I can listen to "Crazy" by Gnarles Barkley as I slowly go insane.
Why get a cell phone? I mean, let's say you're hiking and you fall down a steep slope, knocking yourself unconscious for a few days. When you wake up, your cell phone will be dead - what use then?
And why get a laptop? I mean, let's say you're paratrooping into North Korea, your parachute doesn't open, and you barely get your spare open before you hit the ground, so you're alive but with broken legs. You have your laptop so you have a way of getting help, but there are no wireless networks around! Useless! Why would someone ever get a laptop? What possible use could it be?
And why wear pants? I mean, let's say you're running from a serial killer through an unchartered jungle in the Congo when you're captured by indigenous cannibals. You might be able to use your pants to strangle one of them, but the tribe took them away from you - what possible use are pants if they just get taken away when you need them? That's why I don't buy pants.

In fewer words:
There is a set of objects you should bring on excursions into the forest, and an iPhone is not one of them.
Taking your iPhone camping is like bringing your bagpipes to the movies.

Don't make decisions about buying something based on what functions it doesn't have or what dumb circumstances it can't help you avoid.
"I'm not going to buy an iPhone because it can't deflect bullets or control people's minds." -321southpaw

but here is a rundown of the other things:

smilies
Are you talking about how the smilies always appear at the bottom of a post when you click on them? That happens for everyone. If it is annoying you, then when you click on the "Show all smilies" button then just add in the code for the smily you want. That is usually what I do.

spoiler
If you want to know how a spoiler works, there are some things that become frustrating when you first try to use them (believe me I spent over an hour figuring it out).
When you make spoilers in your forum post and then click "Preview post" it doesn't show the actual spoilers. Instead it gives the code for the spoilers, which can really throw some people off. Don't worry about that. Some things that may help are:
Spoiler: When you make a spoiler with a name you have to type "spoiler=" and then type the text you wantNow I have made a spoiler. I can put whatever I want in here.
to end the spoiler I put "/spoiler" (replace the quotations with brackets). That is pretty much it. Don't worry if the Post Preview doesn't show you the spoiler, they do that so that you can see all the text or images or whatever you have put in.


Hope that helps! Let me know or someone else know if you are still having trouble.

I will edit this post with judging because I don't have a lot of time, I just had enough to do the first couple.


chaosraider
========
Aesthetics: 4/5
Gameplay: 12/15
Difficulty (The harder, the better): 7/10
Simplicity (Little tiles, few objects, etc.): 10/10
---
Total: 33/40

I liked the map, but it seemed a little too... I don't know the word for it, but it was cramped. maybe a little more space to move around would have made it more enjoyable for me. There was really only one way to beat this map, but I did enjoy it nonetheless. good job.
____________________

Animator
========
Aesthetics: 2/5
Gameplay: 10/15
Difficulty: 3/10
Simplicity: 8/10
---
Total: 23/40

The map could have used more... a lot more. There was not very much of a challenge here, but I think you will get the hang of it. There were no mines, which was weird to see in a simple challenge map. It was too easy, and getting an AGD didn't provide as much of a challenge as it should have. Again, adding mines would have helped the difficulty and gameplay aspects.
____________________

kkStrong0
========
Aesthetics: 3/5
Gameplay: 7/15
Difficulty: 8/10
Simplicity: 9/10
---
Total: 27/40

I like the idea of moving drones from one side of the room to the other. It provides a challenge but it also gets annoying. I was able to move the drones from one side of the map to the other one time. Every other time the drones from the left side would then move over to the right side again, and it was very long and tedious. I also felt the trap doors were a little oddly placed, since they didn't do much for the map. If they had done something to change the pattern of the drones that would have been one thing.

EDIT: (Judging continued...)

seven two
========
Aesthetics: 3/5
Gameplay: 13/15
Difficulty: 9/10
Simplicity: 10/10
---
Total: 35/40

WOAH!!! I just beat this map right before I did the judging. This was hard. Not insanely too difficult, but very hard. I don't know what to say, I guess you have to play the map to really get it. It is really addictive when you are playing it and you keep getting closer and closer to the door, but you aren't quite there yet. A good hook for sure.
____________________

lord_day
========
Aesthetics: 4/5
Gameplay: 13/15
Difficulty: 9/10
Simplicity: 9/10
---
Total: 35/40

This level was a challenge. I liked how it wasn't just a straightforward jump to get to the switch; it took some skill. The aesthetics of this map seem to all be in the tileset, which it looks like you spent a little bit of time on. I liked it, and it didn't really take anything away from the map itself because it didn't affect the gameplay. Nice job.
____________________

George
========
Aesthetics: 2/5
Gameplay: 11/15
Difficulty: 6/10
Simplicity: 10/10
---
Total: 29/40

It was... weird. Like ATFB said on NUMA, it is innovative, but not very hard. I liked the level, and it has its purpose, which I can see, I just leave myself wishing there was more, kinda like watching Matrix Reloaded.
____________________

AMLT
========
Aesthetics: 3/5
Gameplay: 12/15
Difficulty: 4/10
Simplicity: 7/10
---
Total: 26/40

Sorry that it is judged low, but I feel this map could have been more thought out. The difficulty isn't great if you cheat, and cheating becomes attractive to those who can't finish it the way it seems to have been planned out. Simplicity is nice. I rated gameplay high because if you do it the way it is supposed to be done it makes a great map.
____________________

azjps

@TheJuggler:
dude... I feel sorry for you. Not a lot of pleasant dreams? I wish you many pleasant dreams. Sleep for me is the only way it seems I can actually escape the world I am in. For you though, it seems like it just continues.


My dream... I have only had this dream once, which makes it the most significant in my life. Every other dream I have had the same dream or something close to it.


I am looking up at the ceiling because there is a beautiful painting at the top. On this painting there are about 3 or 4 cherubs, each with bows and arrows and with a very deep and mysterious blue cloth running between their legs to hide their genitalia. The clouds and the sky painted behind them are more dull to bring out the cherubs, and it is breathtaking. I then look at the walls and am surprised to see they are all gold. Pure gold. The light coming in from the windows reflects off of the gold and creates a lightshow dancing across the walls. Each section of this church is done ornately, and so I look to the floor to see the stone marble. It is not shiny like marble you buy at the granite store, no this is just blocks, much like a sidewalk, but it compliments the walls perfectly. As I look back I see my cousin, a person who I am really close to and share many secrets with, running between my family members who are all lined up to take a picture. My cousin and I are running and not standing still for the picture, but eventually we peek our heads through and we manage to make it into the picture.

This is where my dream ends. It is surprising to me that I have never had this dream again in my life, and the fact that I had it at such a young age makes me think this is significant and that I should find this church if it exists. I do have an idea:
My mom and dad used to live in Italy before they came back to the US just before I was born. Once they were walking in a park and had taken all the paths shown on the park map. When they were about to leave my mom blurts out "We need to go see the church." Upon looking at the map there is no church shown. So they ask an Italian if there is a church somewhere and the Italian points them toward the top of a hill. They travel up this hill and lo and behold there is a church, which my mom immediately recognizes, even though she has never seen this church and didn't know it existed before she thought of it. I believe this is the church that is in my dream. Mind you I am not even born yet, so I have never seen this church.

anyway, yeah, that is all.

#344505 18 2007-07-18T17:00:16Z southpaw
I'm trying to show the "only one future outcome for everything" part of determinism, not that every action we perform is dependent upon the past and the present. It isn't. If you look at a person's past and find that they almost drowned when they were younger there could be two outcomes to this situation:

1. The person never swims again because they are fearful of drowning.
2. The person receives swimming lessons and removes their fear.

Each possibility has at least two choices a person can make. Yes, each choice will have one outcome, but to say the universe is acting upon every individual within it, whether on Earth or in the Andromeda galaxy or elsewhere, is.... well, I don't really have an argument because the counterargument would be "Yes it does!" With the swimming example, you may say the person who chose to take swimming lessons had a different mindset than someone who had the same experience and chose never to swim again.

I guess what I am pretty much trying to say is that individuals are not acting in a manner that is predetermined from the beginnings of the universe but rather we are all given the free will to do as we please, and that in turn is working towards a single outcome. We can change this outcome if we change ourselves, which makes the future a very malleable(?) yet intangible thing.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, 2007-07-18T17:58:03Z
Now what you're describing is basically what I would refer to as Libertarianism.

I think you have me confused for someone else. If I go by your definitions I see that I am arguing for a correlation between determinism and free will, therefore a compatibilist. I recognize that their is going to be one outcome for the future. But I don't think that our actions are what determines this future. This future is bigger than we can control and so our free will can act independently from a determined future, while determinism works on its own course. For example (this is a bad example): The second coming of Jesus, if you believe it will happen. What are we supposed to do about that? Not a lot. It is out of our control, but if it is determined to happen it will.

The end of the world? How do we stop our planet from becoming a black hole? We can't, that is out of our control. We are also drifting toward the sun. Are we going to put giant rockets on the Earth and push the planet a little farther away? I doubt it. So my argument is this, in case that didn't make a lot of sense:

We have free will that allows humans and other beings to do as they want. At the same time there are forces in the universe that are bigger than we can control, so they are determined to happen. If we are not in control then determinism takes over, whereas if we are in control then free will prevails.

I found I was thinking this today when I was coming home on the pubilc bus:

Why was I on the bus? There was one reason I was on the bus and that reason was to go home. Therefore the cause of going home spurred the effect of getting on the bus.

Now, there are two bus routes I could take to get home. But one gets me home faster and right in front of my house. Therefore there is a reason I would take the faster route because it has two bonuses.

Now, then there was the option of not taking a bus home at all and just sitting around downtown. But I didn't choose this option. Some part of me wanted to go home.

I was consciously making decisions that were determined by my want to be in a more familiar place. I had options, I chose one. To say this was predetermined would be a convincing argument though, seeing as how wanting to go home as my cause spurred the effect of me getting there. But I was also in control. I was thinking on the bus that maybe free will is an illusion to keep us happy, kind of like what Daddaluma is saying.

As we get older I believe our need to be different takes the better of us, and so we think we are making decisions that define us seperately from our parents or our family. Those could be determined as happening because we see things in our parents that we dislike or don't want to portray. Striving to be like our friends we find things that we have in common with our peers, determined to fit in. This is all in our self-control, we can all actively see the choices and paths that lie ahead of us. Maybe these choices are just illusions of our desires. Each one may spawn a different outcome and so determines a small or large part of our lives.

I can see now Demonz how the idea of determinism fits into our lives. I couldn't before, but something I realized is that being able to determine an outcome would be impossible unless you were able to view each and every aspect of each and every action, at which point even then a random outlier could occur. Maybe this outlier was determined to happen but how could we measure it? How could we possibly see something so seemingly random that we happened to miss it?

Consciousness on the other hand makes me think of when a person has rights. a new wallpaper. a little pixelated in one part, but I like it just because of the colors and stuff. what do you think?


@xdude:

The first background was pretty simple.

1. I took the last brush in AxeRaider's Radon brush set and set the color to black.
2. I made a second layer and found a blue color that I liked and made it offset slightly.
3. I took the seventh brush from the Litihium brush set, made it white and layered it over the Radon brush.
4. Used the magic wand and selected the Lithium brush. Then I chose both Radon brush layers and erased the selection.
5. Deselect. Then used the blur tool over the erased section.
6. Did some crazy editing by erasing parts of the Lithium brush to make it look like it was part of the Radon brushes.
7. used some other brush in a set by AxeRaider for the part in the top left. Made a selection that was 3 pixels away from the border and used Stroke to make the inner border.

Oh, the best part: make original dimensions 640x580, then blow it up to 1024x768.

#348911 9 2007-07-30T05:55:12Z southpaw
haha, this is my kind of topic. I just did a paper on second language aquisition and how one language differs from another.

To start, let us use the Sapir-Whorf Hypotheses (more commonly reffered to as the Whorf Hypothesis if you are going to look it up on Google), which states that a persons language is like a barrier, one that limits a persons thoughts to the extent of that language. At the surface level this may seem like a pretty strange argument but let us delve into it.

Edward Sapir was the person who first discovered the fact that Inuits or Eskimos had multiple words for snow. There has been some debate but I think that Inuits have one word for one type of snow, and they just happened to define 9 types (like powdery snow, icy snow, melting snow, etc.).

Benjamin Lee Whorf was Sapir's student, and one of the more interesting things he discovered was the idea that a person who knew only one language could express their thoughts to a certain point and then they were left without words. Let us say this person spoke English and was trying to explain their thoughts on some issue. Whorf found that some languages had untranslatable words that helped people who spoke other languages reflect on the given idea more thoroughly because these words thought in the abstract sense. Whorf believed that this kind of difference in expressing thoughts led to a difference in the way people constructed their thoughts when they spoke.

I'll elaborate more when I find my paper, but this is basically what I can remember so forgive me if there are any mistakes. I'll post my paper once I find it.

at the core yes, your brain thinks based on thoughts coming in from your 5 senses. But what about philosophy? Things that have no tangible substance like deities? How is it we can reflect on the idea that gods are responsible for everything around us if we have never seen/heard/felt/tasted/smelled them? We have given shape and form to our gods but in human shape so we can feel like we relate to them more. The five senses do influence our thoughts. But we are talking more in the idea that thought differs among people who speak different languages.

Quote: mosh, 2007-07-30T03:00:15Z
do we all think in the same language, but just interpret it differently?

No, we do not all think in the (edit)exact(/edit) same language. The reason behind this is the fact that we use our language to form our thoughts and languages have different rules. You wouldn't translate the phrase "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" word for word in Spanish or Japanese because it wouldn't make sense to them. Their thoughts follow the rules of their languages. Had they made up their own language they would have their own rules.
The three things that are present in all correct sentences are SUBJECT, VERB, OBJECT in that order.

I ran to the store. subject=I verb=ran object=store

In different languages the subject-verb-object setup is ordered differently. In some languages it goes verb-object-subject, or object-subject-verb, and in some cases there are certain sentences that may contain only a verb and object, or only a subject and object.

As skyline said, we (edit)think according to what our senses tell us(/edit). And the way we interpret it is different, but we are also limited in how we interpret it. I mean, a person who grew up in the jungles of Brazil and had never seen a phone would have a hard time explaining what a phone was to others in his camp if they had never seen a phone. And trying to explain what it does and how it works would be ten times more difficult.

What I mean, using that eskimo/snow example, is that any human will be able to know just as much as any eskimo about snow, even if they have completely different languages. Every minute difference in snow that would mark a different word for the eskimos can easily be reduced to an observable property. The fact that they've been around snow long enough to care about such minute differences doesn't mean they have a greater potential for understanding all that is snow - it just means they're more knowledgeable about it for the same reason that Americans are more knowledgeable than eskimos about CPU architectures.

I believe it is the fact that Eskimos grew up around snow, so naturally they would create many words for the different types of snow because they would need to explain the dangers and benefits of each while hunting. The eskimos can explain the differences in snow much more clearly than a person whose language evolved in a warm place like Africa where snow is only up on the mountain. The language had to evolve around the food source and so African languages grew up in warm places, which I'll bet if you studied the language they can describe certain things about the landscape around them in their language than an Eskimo can in his language, and vice versa.

The idea is that even though a human can describe snow as well as any other human the language would require brand new words to describe this difference because the current language would limit voicing their thoughts. They could probably think about it in their head in these ineffable terms as you pointed out, but trying to explain it would only be possible in the simplest of terms. I was curious to know how we all see ourselves. I know that this may seem weird at first but I think it is important to take a step back from our front that we put up and look at ourselves from a realistic point of view. Your role in your family; how you function in society; what you think or have heard of what your friends think of you, as well as what your first impressions of people are and what you think of your friends; how your beliefs and faith affect how you act and who you interact with; your ideas of how things should work, how family should work; what concerns you for the future, the past, the present; your deepest fears and your greatest triumphs, and so on and so forth. Just an analysis of who you are as a person. I would like each person to take their time as well and not just write down "I think my family loves me." Instead take the time to look at what part you play in the lives of others, including yourself.

RULES

- None of the following should happen in this topic:
  • Harassment of any kind

b_t is saying that the story shows there is no ultimate truth.

What I took away from the story was much simpler in that we are all ignorant in one way or another. We believe things that may not be real, yet we still think they are. Then to be shown what is real and what isn't we have to be forced in some way to see the truth, or the "light of the sun." This can be blinding at first and we don't want to believe what is shown to us at first because we are so accustomed to our own beliefs. But as our eyes become adjusted to the light of the sun so does our knowledge.

Socrates does also say in this story that there are two ways your eyes may be blinded at first: coming from the dark into the light, and also coming from the light into the dark. People can make you believe things that are not true (take Hitler for example). The overall message is agnosticism, but underneath this message there are more profound ones I believe.


Such as this one: What is Socrates saying in the ways of teachers and educators? Does one truly have to be forced into the "light?"

#350393 40 2007-08-02T21:57:15Z southpaw
Quote: Ethrel, August 02, 2007 04:53 pm
The only problem with dealing with someone who had those senses at one point would be that they had already had time to learn to 'think' in those senses, and there would be major parts of their thinking process that would be left untouched due to unconscious habit. IMO, of course.

But habits can be broken. Your brain is systematic, so that as long as something is being frequently used it thinks it is important. If you suddenly stop seeing your brain starts to forget visual memory because it no longer sees that as important (pun slightly intended). Your brain won't forget it all at once, nor will it forget all of it, but you will lose a lot of your ability to store visual information. If you happen to get your sight back, then your brain will start receiving information through your eyes again and start that visual memory up again. Although a person who had only one sense would be ideal for testing this, it would not be much of a long shot to test someone who had been born with the other four senses.

I could read when I was almost 3. And I was a pretty good reader too. Anyway, so the next year I was put into preschool and had this really great teacher who was very patient and seemed to know exactly how you felt. Well she was pregnant and told us one day that she had to leave to have her baby and that she wasn't going to be coming back.
The next week we had a substitute teacher while they found a permanent employee. This lady who was our sub was a f***ing B*tch. One day I was sitting there with a book reading it, in my head. Of course when you are three and you say you can read nobody believes you, so she didn't believe me. But the thing she did wrong was tell me that I couldn't read. If she had said, "Okay, you just keep reading then," I would have been fine. But no, I tell her I'm reading in my head and she tells me I can't read. Then when I actually start reading to her she tells me I can be put in a timeout for lying. It still pisses me off, and I'm not sure why because it was such a long time ago, but after that I stopped bonding so much with teachers and authority figures.

Quote: usaswim, August 04, 2007 07:30 pm
I just love your color choices so much... tell me your secret ;_;

haha, there isn't really a secret so much as experiment. I mean, when I am doing color choices I go through almost the entire color wheel looking for something, seriously. When you are making your image don't think so much of the color until you have the right brush. I think for Smort's especially I used about three or four different abstract brushes before I found the one I wanted, which took about a minute. Then once I found the one I wanted I just kept stepping backwards and then set the brush on the canvas a couple times to see what a new color or modification to the brush looked like. That step took about ten minutes.

If that was confusing in any way here is a much simpler version to choosing colors:

Take the color of the background or a part of a brush that had a gradient type to it. Then open up your color picker and don't do anything except move the little circle around and finding something you think might look good. If the color doesn't work then choose a different color using the same method. If after a while you still haven't found a decent color, move the bar on the side up or down a little bit. Usually you can find a color that works just by slight changes with the color wheel.

Hope that helps

a rundown of my favorite vegetables cooked in the best ways, according to me:

Onions - When you make beef and add onions to it, it is really good. Wait until the onions are a ilttle burnt. This makes them crispy and they are covered in beef fat.

Sweet Potatoes (or Yams) - shave the skin off and then lay them flat in the bottom of a glass casserole or baking dish. Add a mixture of orange juice and brown sugar, and a little butter I think, but I'm not entirely sure, and also add cranberries. Heat them in the oven. I don't know how hot, but probably until the yams get hot.

Lemon Cucombers - Cut into slices and add salt.
Tomatoes - see above

Sweet Peas - Eat them plain. They are juicy and great. Wash them first tho.

Carrots - Plain or cooked, but if you cook them make sure they are soft.

Celery - I only like it if it has Peanut Butter and nothing else. My mom tried to make me eat it with cream cheese and raisins, but I would always trade those to the kids who had better food. For some reason they enjoyed my food more.

I think that is it... And stirfry would have to include pretty much all of these except the yams and cucombers.

What is a smurf anyway? Why are they in existence? The answer to this question was best answered by Dr. Byuilgyt, a French scientist who was an avid watcher of the show. He said that a "smurf is not like any other creature. Their closest relatives come from the leprechaun, which died out hundreds of years before the smurf show ever aired." He then continued on to say "Every person who has seen a smurf in real life has died at some point in time in the future. They are dangerous creatures and to make them into happy cartoon characters is the most common misconception of who they really are."
Doubt has come up in the Smurfologist society about whether a smurf can be captured. Eventually a woman named Cisco Flur, a Romanian, figured out a way to capture a smurf in a humane fashion and be able to study it. Her device was called food-in-a-cage, and you can see the device has been used for many other capturings of dangerous animals. Unfortunately smurf's only eat fingernail clippings (which is why they are most abundant near landfills where fingernail clippings get dropped everyday), and a sufficient number of clippings was not present at the time of the date set for capture. Cisco lost all her funding and was murdered by an anonymous killer.
By the 18th Century smurfs were running wild through the streets of towns in Europe, killing cats and other animals smaller than an elephant. Humans were dropping like flies. It is said that smurf turns black right before it kills somebody, and it is a fallcious statement to say that a disease is what caused the Black Plague. No, it was smurfs.
In the beginning of the 19th century near a small cottage in the plains of Scotland a smurf was sneaking up on a cat. The smurf was unaware however that the cat was the famed Asriel, killer of smurfs. This cat would be depicted as mean and awful in the cartoons, but he was truly a blessing to the countryside of Scotland, who was able to eliminate their smurf problem by 1822. None of his paintings have survived, save one, which shows Asriel sitting on a chair with a smurf in his mouth, green blood dripping from its severed arms.
Eventually smurfs retired to the places of trash and such. Not a smurf has been seen in over 150 years, except for one incident when a smurf came out from underneath the trash in a landfill and attacked a man who was dumping only fingernail clippings into the landfill. This attack was recorded in 1932, and the man was able to grab a hold of the smurfs neck and choke it to death. When the police asked about it the man said the smurf turned a bright green that glowed from within its body. And this is how we know smurfs turn green when you choke them.

Step 1: Go to deviantArt.com

Step 4: Experiment

well I don't know if you have heard of population bottlenecks. It is quite interesting in that some scientists believe that there was a vast number of genetic differences among humans in the early years of evolution. Through certain factors that decreased the population more than 50% people were forced to inbreed to keep their tribes and clans alive, due to the lack of breeding partners available.

Mitochondrial DNA is only inherited from your mother, and the Y-chromosome is inherited from your father. Some believe that there were many variations of mitochondrial DNA and the Y-chromosome, but after the population was decreased considerably these variations were decreased too and may be the reason why there is so little genetic variation among humans. This is the Wikipedia game that I have created with me and a friend.

Objective
Try and get from one topic to the next in the least amount of clicks.

Rules

1. You can only use the links inside of Wikipedia to get to your destination. Clicking on a link to some other website like Google and connecting back to Wikipedia is not okay.
--
2. No clicking the back button (I can't really enforce this one but please use the honor system). You may only click the back button once you have come to your target destination, at which point you should record your steps.
--
3. Once you have made it to the target page record your progress backwards. For example...
If I were to record my progress from "Grass" to "Infusion" I would put - Infusion>Tea>lemongrass>Grass


And that is it. If you have any questions just post them here. I will try and set up a new challenge every week, but please bear with me. I will post the challenge and at the end of that week the person who has discovered the shortest route will win a... DED map. just for fun.

Do not PM me with any submissions. Only post them here. If someone copies someone else's route, the first person to post the route will get the recognition, so don't sweat posting it here. Thanks.

--------------------

Week 1 Challenge - Go from China to Tetrahedron in the least number of clicks.

Quote: http://www.fema.gov/hazard/dproc.shtm
    * Local Government Responds, supplemented by neighboring communities and volunteer agencies. If overwhelmed, turn to the state for assistance;

    * The State Responds with state resources, such as the National Guard and state agencies;

    * Damage Assessment by local, state, federal, and volunteer organizations determines losses and recovery needs;

    * A Major Disaster Declaration is requested by the governor, based on the damage assessment, and an agreement to commit state funds and resources to the long-term recovery;

    * FEMA Evaluates the request and recommends action to the White House based on the disaster, the local community and the state's ability to recover;

    * The President approves the request or FEMA informs the governor it has been denied. This decision process could take a few hours or several weeks depending on the nature of the disaster.
FEMA must get a Major Disaster Declaration by the governor, which didn't happen the first day. Then they must recommend action to the White House, then the President must approve it.

#358585 8 2007-08-23T06:56:15Z southpaw
haha, this is where the Allegory of the Cave comes into play.

Ignorance is defined by Socrates as when a man who has seen shadows all his life is shown what is "true" in a sense, and yet that man denies it. At first he would rather believe the shadows on the cave are the truths in his life. But if he is returned to his shackles and stares at the walls his mind will think of the objects, the real objects shown to him, and he will not be able to deny that they were not of a real sort, just as the shadows are real.

At first he was content knowing that the shadows on the cave were the "truth." How can you know you are blissful if you have never known anything else besides your knowledge up to the point at which you decided to be ignorant? Because an infant doesn't decide they are ignorant from day one. There comes a point where they accept all the knowledge they have received, which comes much later in life, and they decide they are content with what they agree with and sometimes try to change the things they do not agree with. Therefore, nobody knows true ignorance because we are all taught different things and are shoved into situations we have never encountered. True ignorance would be someone who has seen only "shadows" their whole lives, never being told what is right and wrong, and making their own judgement on things. This has probably only occured a few times, and it was before humans were ever dealing with philosophy, probably when humans started to emerge on this planet is my guess.

#358712 33 2007-08-23T18:21:05Z southpaw
Quote: Obby, August 23, 2007 10:39 am
The same way that the background in Da Vinci's Mona Lisa is offset?

My point is, these people knew what they were doing. Because of their religious fervor, they wouldn't have picked random numbers.

I cannot find an argument against that. But let me say what I have continued to say:

Numbers are only important to the people they influence. In the western worlds, 7 is a divine number, a lucky number. But as I said, 52 was the divine number for the Aztecs who had to sacrifice someone every 52 years to ensure the sun rose the next day. Did you know the Aztecs knew the earth was round? They had a very advanced mathematical system which was all but lost when the Spanish came through and wiped out most of their civilization. We divide our weeks up into 7 days (no surprise how that came to be) and we have 12 months (again, no surprise). But that is only because the church influenced the Gregorian calendar.

Now take a look at Aztec calendars:
Quote: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec_calendar
The tonalpohualli ("day count") consists of a cycle of 260 days, each day signified by a combination of a number from one to thirteen, and one of the twenty day signs. With each new day, both the number and day sign would be incremented: 1 Crocodile is followed by 2 Wind, 3 House, 4 Lizard, and so forth up to 13 Reed, after which the cycle of numbers would restart, giving 1 Jaguar. The cycle of twenty day signs, however, would continue until 7 Flower, after which it would restart and give 8 Crocodile. It would take a full 260 days (1320) for the two cycles of twenty day signs and thirteen numbers to realign and repeat the combination 1 Crocodile.

This their 260 day ritual cycle, or day count. Notice that they count 13 numbered days, something that would have never been condoned by the Church, seeing as how Friday the 13th wasn't exactly a good day. The Aztecs also had a calendar of years that went for 365 days, something they figured out on their own, which I find amazing.

Quote: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiuhpohualli
The Aztec solar year was divided into 18 "months" of twenty days each, called in Spanish veintenas, with an addition of an extra five days at the end.

So you see, the numbers for the Aztec faith were given by the people, even though they had strong beliefs and fears of their gods. I'm sure if we were all Aztec peoples we would view 5 as a bad number because the last 5 days of the year were called "nothing days" and if a child was born on one of these days they would consider this child to amount to nothing in its life. Whether these numbers came from the divine words of their gods is debatable, but just to show you that numbers are arbitrary and only affect those who know of them and have been influenced by them.

Pretty much I'm just really curious to know what comes after death. He told me that there is no point in trying to find out about death without living. It is a mystery that can wait.

this was a good point but it didn't reassure me. I'm not going to kill myself, don't worry about it. Everybody thinks of suicide at some point. There is no reason not to. Some just take their thoughts to reality. Not something I would necessarily condone but not something I look down upon either.


Anyway, I live for... nothing. There is no reason that I am living. Actually that isn't true. I'm waiting for the day I realize what my life is for. Looking for meaning is pointless but I do it anyway.

I think I live only because my animal instincts are telling me not to do anything rash. I go to school and it is a big waste of time because I end up failing classes. My family has always held high expectations of me as the first born child, as well as first born son in my generation, while I have three female cousins and a sister who all have expectations but they don't seem as elevated as mine are. I decided a long time ago how much I hated expectations and it was at this point that I started to fail school. I got straight D's for 8th grade. My sophomore year I managed to get three F's before dropping out. My only A was in chemistry.

Things have been getting a little better but I am also starting to repeat the same habits. I enrolled in an alternative program to finish high school and was doing really well for the first three terms and then somehow I've managed to fail two college classes so far and have one Incomplete I must finish. Education is a must in this society and I feel like I'm not getting conventional methods.

I started piano about a 2 1/2 years ago and I love it. I could make a career of music if I want, but this requires education...

I do have family. My parents divorced when I was younger, but they both found someone else and my family doubled in size. But these expectations bear down on me. The only people I feel that have expectations of me but don't constantly pressure me about them are my grandparents.

so I have my family to live for, even though they proceed to pester me with how I should be doing so well in school because I'm so smart and that I am capable of passing all my classes. I don't think my mom is a very good parent for me, maybe my sister, but not me.


anyway, pretty much I'm saying that my family is what I have to live for, and the thought that one day I might become old and have lived a long but not necessarily happy life and die.

I have been pondering the question of whether racism is a necessary part of our society or not, what is the extent of its power, and how it really affects individuals. For one, I have noticed that racism is not easily brought up in conversation with people. If they are for racism then they express it blatantly in situations where they feel comfortable, probably with people they know who might share the same views. If they are against racism they only talk of things that need to be done to remove racism instead of the actual thing itself.

So my question is this:

Would bringing racism out in the open actually help remove ideas of racism, or would it generate more hate towards those being targeted?


My answer, and the one I am sticking by, is that racism should be brought up, especially in school. I believe that what many racist people don't realize is that they have created this fear of people who are different than them just because of the color of their skin, or the shape of their eyes, or even the size of their genitals. By talking about it they might realize just how indifferent each person is with one another, and may eventually come to an understanding.

Here is a short list of things that I am talking about (none of which I agree with):
  • Black people like fried chicken
  • White people have small penises
  • Asians don't drive well because their eyes are slanted and therefore cannot see as good
  • All Mexicans have crossed the border illegally
  • Jewish people are rich because they steal money
  • All peoples from the Middle East are terrorists
In addition to answering the question, if you could maybe give an example of a time when you witnessed racism then that would be great.

And mods... I know this is a very touchy topic. I would like to see some responses though and have this thing not be locked just because of potential flaming.

==Week 1==
This weeks theme is Canyons. Make a map that has a canyon aspect to it. The entries are due Sunday, September 16th, 2007 by midnight. If all entries are in before the deadline the next round will start, so that way there isn't a huge delay.

Welcome to the FIVER competition, where the object of the game is to get a five on a single map... the twist? oh right, the twist. Get a perfect five from three of the five judges... heh heh heh...


Here are the rules:

1. NO OLD MAPS. Anybody found using an old map will not be considered for judging.
2. You may submit your maps here in this thread, either as a link to NUMA or a *.txt file.
3. Each week you will be judged on the overall level, like on NUMA. But remember that each judge may be particular about certain things, so it is important to consider gameplay, tileset, object placement, enemy placement, difficulty, etc when making your map.
4. The judges will rate the map according to what they would rate it on NUMA.
5. Those who recieve a 5 from at least three of the five judges will win the grand prize. The is an ongoing contest. Each round is 8 weeks. If nobody has recieved at least three 5's then we revert to the lower prize table (see below).
6. Each week will be a different theme. The themes will be according to style, such as action, puzzle, etc.
7. N art and tilesets are not allowed (for obvious reasons), but DDA's are. If the theme happens to be "Prisoner Maps" and you make a DDA based off a prisoner map then be my guest and submit it.


Contestants are encouraged to spend time on their maps.

I will need 5 judges who will be able to judge each and every week. There will be one extra judge (me) who will rate the judges maps. Contestants are unlimited. You may join at any point in the competition.

This is an ongoing competition. Those who may recieve fives from at least three of the judges will recieve the grand prize but the contest will continue, so in this way the competiton doesn't end.
Also, the rounds will be in 8 week intervals. Each week will have a different theme you will have to follow. At the end of the eight weeks the prizes are given out to those who scored the highest. But the next week a new 8 week round starts again, allowing those who didn't make it on the last round to try again. And so it continues.


The Grand Prize:
1 Dedication map
Your choice of (1) a sigatar set or (2) a second dedication map

The Prize Table:
1st place - Your choice of a DED or a sigatar set. You also get a sig bar saying you got first.
2nd place - Your choice of a DED or a sigatar set
3rd place - A DED

For those of you confused about the prize table:
The grand prize is only for those who receive three 5's. The Prize Table is for the rounds. If a person gets three 5's in the 4th week they get the grand prize, and can still compete in the contest. At the end of the eight weeks the scores are tallied up and the prizes given to 1st, 2nd and 3rd place are determined by the Prize Table. If you have won the grand prize you are eligible to win it again in consecutive rounds, as well as eligible to win any of the prizes from the Prize Table at the end of each round.

Oh, unrelated grammatical point: you misused "it's" both in the picture and in your post here.
That happens to be probably one of my worst grammar problems to date. I can never remember where the apostrophe is supposed to be used

But still, it's a nice change.

The usage of "it's" and "its"

When talking of things as they should be, as in saying "it is" or "it has" you can shorten that to become "it's"

"It is a nice day" can be changed to "It's a nice day."
"It has become dangerous" can be changed to "It's become dangerous."

When using "it" and you are saying "its" ask yourself first if the sentence, when spelled out fully, reads the "its" as an "it is." if so put the apostrophe. If not then put the S afterward.

"Its candid behavior was annoying."

I don't know if that helps. maybe.

when you are finished playtesting and all do the following:

#363942 78 2007-09-10T16:07:42Z southpaw
To try and sum up what Demonz is saying:

There is no ultimate truth. Humans have not discovered an ultimate truth, so it is silly to think that everything we do must be acted upon with a "complete" knowledge of our actions. (Did I sum that up or did I just say something entirely different?)

See b_t not even you can claim that "truth" is at all relevant, as "truth" is a fallacy of the mind. What you claim to be "true" is just the observation of a pattern which may be broken at one point, in which case you readjust your idea of "true."

Here is an example:
A man goes to the bar everyday to drink tequila. Is it true that he drinks tequila every time he enters the bar? As much as we know about the man so far, yes we can assume it is true.
This goes on for five years. We pretty much know by now that the man is going to enter the bar to drink tequila. But suddenly the man decides to quit drinking. He enters the bar and you assume because of a pattern that he is going to drink tequila because you have not discovered yet that the man has decided to quit drinking. Suddenly your idea of truth about the man is changed. Now the truth about the man is that he will not drink tequila because he has decided to quit drinking. Because of the connotation of quiting drinking, you assume he doesn't drink at all anymore, but you see him stumble out of the bar slobbering drunk. It is no longer true that he has quit drinking. Instead he now drinks a kind of pale ale. your idea of what is "true" of the man has changed many times because of what you have heard of him.
Let's say you were the bartender. You see the man walk in and you immediately start to pour him a shot of tequila because of a pattern you have observed. You have not heard that the man has decided to quit drinking, yet you are pouring him a shot of tequila because you have "faith" (as defined by numero UNO in Demonz post) that he will drink it. You find out that the man has quit drinking, yet you followed through with an action because you assumed something was true of the man.

Make sense? hopefully that does. Now we can get back on topic unless Dave wants to shoot down my example. And please correct me if I'm not saying what I think you are saying Demonz. What I put was what I thought you were trying to say from all your posts.

#364403 6 2007-09-12T05:08:47Z southpaw
I have a problem with your analogy of a robot factory to a tree.

Let me break it down into seperate ideas.

1. You say the robot factory will continue to devote resources to each and every section of the land it is growing on, even the one that is bombed every two weeks. But if you chop a section of tree off for a long enough period of time the tree will stop growing in that section. I realize not every plant is like this (certain shrubs for example continue to grow whether you keep cutting them or not), but for the most part you can cut a limb of a tree over and over until the limb stops growing. In this way the tree has realized it cannot grow there and shows some form of sentience that lines up with one of your three aspects of what sentience is.

2. For the section to the east. Your analogies didn't match up. If a tree were to grow right into a sandbox with no shade it would literally have no resources except those that were coming in from the tree itself. I suggest you make it so that it has very little mineral content or some sun. If it had the latter the tree would make a new sprout to capture that sunlight. So the robot analogy would have to stick with it and the robots would have to start making a factory similar to the central one whose purpose is to spread out, at which point the factory in the east would send other resources to the central factory, just like the new sprout would send small amounts of sugars to the main trunk.

Everything else for the tree section lined up for me and made sense.

Now to the bugs and cats and rocks...

If sentience was simply:
Quote: tsukatu, 2007-09-12T01:49:24Z
-a mechanism to perceive [external stimuli]
-a mechanism to comprehend the [external stimuli]
-a mechanism that directly adjusts [the thing's] behavior based on [its] comprehension of the [external stimuli]
then most every living thing is sentient, which I don't accept. For me sentience is these things plus two other ideas and they are (1) abstract thinking, and (2) the ability to learn from said external stimuli. Now most creatures who play the part of predator or prey have the latter of the two. They can learn from the information they receive from their parents and from trial and error. A lion cub does not know how to pounce from instinct, but it does learn through watching the hunters pounce, and through trial and error of performing the action of pouncing itself. What the lion doesn't have is abstract thought (and although I cannot prove this I hope I can assume we all agree).
The idea of sentient being to me is the being who can gain knowledge and ponder the use and application of the knowledge, to understand what something is like just from the explanation of it. Being able to think about gravity, something whose only visual clue is when an object falls to the ground, is a good example of abstract thought. Other creatures of this planet do not have this kind of thinking so far as we know, so we can assume they are not sentient. The fact that we are talking about our own ability to understand this kind of abstract information of sentience itself is another sign that we are sentient. anyway...

awaiting your response.

When my mom was 17 and a Junior in high school she got the chance to go on an archeological dig in Jordan. Unfortunately she didn't get to go that year because at the time Jordan was a very unsafe country. She hoped to go the next year, but in case she didn't, her art teacher told her that he was arranging a surprise for her if the archeological dig didn't pan out.
Once again it didn't, and at the end of her senior year in high school she was offered a scholarship to go to design school. She eventually got a job on an Army base and worked as an Arts and Crafts teacher. My mom and dad met on the Army base (my dad was working for the Air Force and was stationed there) and they got married mostly because my dad needed to be married to someone who lived off of the Army base to be allowed to live otuside the base, because he hated the sleeping quarters and all that.
Eventually I was conceived and about 6 or 7 months into my mom's pregnancy, my dad was beign transferred back to the US. My mom wanted to stay in Italy and she told my dad if he wanted to leave that he could come back once he left the Air Force, but instead he was able to have the Army come in and pack all my moms clothes and ship her back to the states against her will because of some Army code. She was so angry at him for that, and she swore to never let my dad try and change her life so drastically again. They made their way back to Portland and lived in a crappy apartment, instead of the small villa that looked out over the Adriatic Sea in Italy. My mom was miserable, and I was born a couple months after they came back.

#17271 1 2007-09-19T07:23:49Z southpaw
This is a speech I did a while ago. Thought some of you may want to comment on the ideas brought up in this.


Bilingual Education

Although we recognize English as the prominent language in America it is not, and has not been declared as our national language. It would be surprising to create that kind of unity and nationalism by making English the official language. America is slowly becoming populated by a Hispanic people. It is estimated sometime within the next 50 years that Whites will no longer be the majority of people within the United States. This is a wake-up call that we should all recognize, that we are all part of a global community. If we cannot communicate with others in this community then we will lose in the long run. This is why it is necessary for children to learn a second language in schools starting at the elementary level.
During the 1980s an issue came to the forefront of American minds: Should English be the official language of America? In 1981 the 97th Congress was faced with a proposal to add an amendment to the constitution making English the official language of the United States. The amendment also made it so that federal and state laws and regulations requiring the use of other languages would have been prohibited (Eschholz 380). Although his English Language Amendment was struck down in the senate his cause to make English the official language was not.
U.S. English, an organization tied closely with Hayakawas cause, was founded in 1983 by Hayakawa and a man named John Tanton. Tanton was an ophthalmologist from Michigan who founded the Federation of American Immigration Control (FAIR). He not only favored English as the national language he also called for tighter control of immigration. As the chairman for English Only, Tanton handpicked its employees and set policy directions. In just five years from 1983 to 1988 English-only had 13 states that made English their official language, and all but two of the fifty states had proposed legislation for making English their official language.
Since the birth of English-only many critics said it had very racial undertones, but they were never able to come up with any evidence. In 1988 that changed when a private document written by Tanton claimed that America was going to be dominated by Hispanics through immigration and high birth rate, in one passage asking Will the present majority peaceably hand over its political power to a group that is simply more fertile?
As you can most likely see the racial bigotry of this statement I am not going to present the counter to that, or else my paper would be about racism through language. To counter this argument I present to you the facts of benefits from learning two languages.
One of the most interesting studies on language involves the Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis, formulated by two linguists, Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf. Their idea of language as a structure of thought leads into many interesting discussions, one of which says language is a restriction to how people view the world and how they voice their thoughts and opinions. Ellen Bialystok shows that the ideas for spatial concepts among English speaking adults and Korean speaking adults differs in that English uses words for space with things that go together, such as rings and hats are put on, apples in bowls and pieces in puzzles are put in, and put together is what happens to Lego pieces. But for Koreans the language they use for these spatial terms differs among what is tight- and loose-fitting. Therefore putting together Legos, rings and puzzle pieces are all defined by one term, while putting on a hat and putting apples in a bowl are phrased by a different term. So how does this benefit children and bilingualism?
One of the key points of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis is that people who know more than one language perceive the world in a much different view. They voice their thoughts and opinions differently because they have connected two languages that may have different ideas of space, time, objects, and even movement. Bialystok claims that this idea is correct in principle but wrong in order. She does not deny though that learning a second language is concept learning as well, that learning a new language in this case changes the way concepts are organized in our mind.
In California, especially Los Angeles, the bilingual education there is failing. Only 5 percent of children classified as not knowing English going into school come out of school with a working knowledge of the English language. This number is a dismal rate and lends a hand to the fact that many parents dont want bilingual education because of horrible success statistics. Many of the California schools claim that it takes a 5-year-old child seven years to learn a new language, based off of the results of their bilingual education. Seven years? I can probably correctly say parents dont want to pay extra for seven years so their child will learn English. Speaking of money, did you know that California schools receive extra funding for each child in their school that comes out not knowing English? It is now wonder the schools are failing in their bilingual programs. This is not only limiting to a childs education it is not fair. Why have bilingual programs that dont work? To have a successful bilingual program it would require benefits for students and schools who are proficient in both languages they are learning.
Generally humans fear what they dont understand. I believe the reason there is an English-only movement in America is because those people dont understand the languages brought into America. We are a diverse culture with diverse people. It is important that we become more accepting of others; to accept them we must understand them; to understand them starts with learning their languages. I would urge you to think about how a second language would benefit children: As China becomes a growing economic power that has many times more people than we do, why not have Chinese available in public schools? By providing a second language to students they will be prepared for the rest of the world. College already requires 2 years of second language; nursing programs require you be somewhat proficient in a second language. You can help prepare the next generation for the world ahead of them, and you can start with second language in schools.



WORKS CITED

Bialystok, Ellen. In Other Words. New York: Basic Books, 1994.

Crawford, James. Hold Your Tongue. New York: Addison-Wesley Publishing Company, 1992.

Eschholz, Paul, Alfred Rosa, Virginia Clark. Language Awareness. Boston: Bedford/St. Martins, 2000.

Unz, Ron K. "English-Only Education Should Be Standard in Most Schools." Bilingual Education. Ed. Loreta Medina. At Issue Series. San Diego: Greenhaven Press, 2003. Opposing Viewpoints Resource Center. Thomson Gale. Multnomah County Library. 9 June 2007 <http://find.galegroup.com/ovrc/infomark.do?&contentSet=GSRC&type=retrieve&tabID=T010&prodId=
OVRC&docId=EJ3010256207&source=gale&srcprod=OVRC&userGroupName=multnomah_main&version=1.0>.

The problem with language is that it is a barrier. You learn the application and use of the language, until you have mastered the language and it is yours. But you are limited to your thoughts by how far you can think in that language. For example, in English we have ordered our senteces in the following way: Subject, Verb, Object. Other languages order their SVO differently, and so you would have to adjust your thought process to understand the order in which the SVO goes. Just sitting there,
Resting, almost asleep,

He cant see,
He knows what coming so he tries to get up,
But trips, and slips,
Farther down the dune,
No grip, but he makes it to the top,
His only thought, is run,
Run, mother f***er, RUN! RUN!
He falls over from the wind force at his back,
The sand is covering him now hes trapped,
Theres no escape,
A while later the storm has passed by,
But the boy is gone, buried deep underground,
Without a trace

Okay...

Quote: http://science.nasa.gov/headlines/y2003/09sep_blackholesounds.htm
In musical terms, the pitch of the sound generated by the black hole translates into the note of B flat. But, a human would have no chance of hearing this cosmic performance because the note is 57 octaves lower than middle-C. For comparison, a typical piano contains only about seven octaves. At a frequency over a million billion times deeper than the limits of human hearing, this is the deepest note ever detected from an object in the Universe.

We cannot register the note created by the black hole but that doesn't mean it isn't making sound.

About the whole, "if I don't perceive it it must not be there" thing.... This is obviously not true. Think of a blind person. Regardless of their inability to perceive light they still perceive the physical surroundings with their sense of touch as well as we do. Just because they cannot see the wall does not mean the wall does not exist. Otherwise blind people would be walking through walls all the time.

You can find the whole article here: http://science.nasa.gov/headlines/y2003/09...kholesounds.htm

#374569 42 2007-10-26T08:54:26Z southpaw
Quote: Atilla, October 26, 2007 05:34 am
Quote: southpaw, October 25, 2007 03:10 pm
About the whole, "if I don't perceive it it must not be there" thing.... This is obviously not true. Think of a blind person...
Perception != sight, as you said you said yourself. Therefore, blind people still perceive things and your example is not relevant.

I was bringing up the point that regardless of whether you can see something or not doesn't mean it isn't there. You can watch a tree fall, but if you don't hear it fall does it still make a sound? Yes. You can also hear a tree fall, but if you didn't see it did it still fall? Yes.

But if you don't hear the tree fall, and you don't see the tree fall, what evidence is there to suggest the tree even fell at all? Simply by testing to make sure that things are still as they seem even if you cannot perceive them.

Try numbing all your senses and walk through a wall, one you are unfamiliar with or that you didn't know existed. Chances are once your senses come back you will realize that you never went through the wall because it managed to exist even though you couldn't perceive it.

#17862 1 2007-11-10T09:14:19Z southpaw
The other day I was thinking about perception, mostly because of the thread started from the question of "If a tree falls in the woods, and nobody is around to hear it, does it still make a sound?"

I don't want anybody to answer this question in this thread, as there is already a thread for that.

On to my point: As I was thinking about reality and watching the sunlight on the floor of my living room I realized something, and that is we are all living in the past.

I thought about this. People have always told me we live in the "present" but as I thought about it more and more there was no possible way that we are perceiving the present. Here's why.


1. Light: Although the rate is a rather small number, our eyes perceive things essentially in frames. For instance, a lightbulb flashes on and off constantly at very rapid speeds. Our eyes are unable to register this flicker, and therefore I assume we see in "frames". Even then, our eyes also have a delayed reaction. For the time it takes light to reach our eyes and the time it takes our brain to process this is a very small amount of time to us, but it shows that things we are viewing have already happened. We are constantly seeing things at a time slightly behind what has actually happened.

2. Touch: The same thing applies here. If you touch a hot pan, there is a slight delay. Even though the time is near instant there is still a delay, so you have essentially touched the pan before your brain registered you have. You have performed an action and your brain is slightly behind in registering it, therefore you have perceived something that has happened in the past.

3. Sound: This is the easiest one to explain, mostly because the farther away you are from a sound the longer it takes for you to hear it, if you hear it at all. The soundwaves have to travel to your eardrum and then your brain has to register this and determine what kind of sound it is. So the sound has already happened while your brain is processing it.

We need not focus on taste and smell because I'd just be repeating myself.

I find this idea quite interesting myself. I just wanted to hear your thoughts. I'd be happy to explain more, but I've just been reflecting and expanding on this idea within the last week.


-southpaw-
#378203 8 2007-11-10T09:36:39Z southpaw
The idea is that regardless of what you are looking at or touching there is always a split second before your brain has realized what the information is. We are constantly perceiving things that have already happened.

Another point is looking at the stars in the sky. They might already be burnt out, but we are only viewing light that has travelled millions of billions of lightyears to reach our eyes. If we shorten this to the sunlight reaching our eyes, first of all it takes approx. 8 minutes for the sunlight to reach Earth. So by the time you see the sun rising it is already 8 minutes ahead of where you have perceived it to be. (heh, that one was for Ignate)

#379186 17 2007-11-13T22:46:46Z southpaw
What it comes down to is this: our bodies and minds are in the present. We truly are always in the present. But we cannot perceive this. It is impossible because of the delay from our brain having to receive a message, determine what it means, then send a reaction. Our perception of what is "the present" is effectively in the past.

Same with a computer. As I type there is a slight delay from the time I hit the key to the time it shows up on the monitor. There is also a slight delay from the time I hit the bottom of the keystroke to the time my brain has made this realization.

What may be more interesting is that our brain has done one of two things. Just so that I can relate to it and explain the idea easier, let's say you are playing piano. Either your brain waits for the message that you have hit a piano key and sends a message to lift the finger but the delay is so quick you don't realize it; or your brain has predetermined the length of the stroke and has sent the message to lift the finger before the message that the key has been hit is received.

I think the former seems more probable, while the latter is more interesting to think about. But I may be wrong.

For me autism is a form of mental retardation, even though many autistic people show specialization in certain skills, such as music, painting, math, etc. In the end, what I'm trying to say is that people who have developed a mental illness over the course of their lifetime through social pressures should be responsible for their actions. People who were born with or became mentally retarded should not be considered entirely responsible for their actions, or we should at least give them more patience than a person with a mental illness.
#381540 60 2007-11-21T18:28:56Z southpaw
Quote: blue_tetris @ Wednesday, 21-Nov-2007, ore 16:54, 2007-11-21T16:54:59Z
Sounds like semantics to me.

People won't be diagnosed with anorexia unless they are unable to control it--like mental retardation or schizophrenia, they can't mandate their own actions some of the time. If you fully understand the function of mental illness, you'd understand that people don't like having them and try very hard to overcome them, like any other disease. I repeat: people won't be diagnosed with a mental illness unless they are unable to regulate it, just as people won't be diagnosed with blindness if they are currently clenching shut their eyes; those things aren't illness unless they disable the patient.

So any mental illness is as inescapable as a broken leg, a weak heart, or a slow liver. Otherwise, it'd not have been diagnosed as an illness.

But what benefit is it to say that anorexics have decided to have their disease? Does this mean we don't have to cure it (because they clearly don't want to be cured)? Does this mean that they are legally responsible for their starvation? Why determine that something is choice unless you want its sufferer to be "guilty" in some regard?

That makes sense.

Let me revise my position.

Anorexia, OCD, clinical depression... They all start out as a choice. But as the choice progresses it becomes habit, it becomes their lifestyle, it becomes a part of who they are, ingrained so deeply that they can no longer control their behavior.

Is that a little closer? I'm trying to find a middle ground because I can see how after a while anorexia or other mental illness is uncontrolable, but in the beginning they start out as a choice.

I took Mo Duk Pai Kung Fu from the time I was 9 until October 2006. I had to go through kids ranks first, which went: white (you start out at white as soon as you start training, but you don't get a sash for it), orange sash, orange-purple, purple, purple-blue, blue, blue-green, green, green-brown, brown, brown-black. That's as far as you go as a kid.

then as an adult you go: white, orange, purple, blue, green, brown, brown-black, black. Then it's just degrees of black belt from there on out. Once you have achieved your second degree black belt you get the title of Sifu.

Quote: SoY, 2007-11-30T15:16:06Z
Karate. Shotokan, I think it was... I'm a black belt. I remember after I did the test and got my belt, the sensei said to me, "You have to remember that this may seem like the end... but it is only the beginning."
I have always had a problem with other styles of martial arts. And I think this finally gives me the reason why. For me it always seemed like other styles quickly advanced you to black belt, and then you started your training for real. In Mo Duk Pai, the average person takes years, I think usually around 5-10 years of training, often around 7 years though, and it felt like you weren't advancing too quickly. I took Tae Kwon Do as well and within 6 months I had advanced 2 ranks. So Mo Duk Pai was a better fit and it allowed me to feel like I was actually advancing to a level that was consistent with how advanced I was in my training.

I think overall martial arts is a good thing to know. Some styles just seem weird at how fast their students advance.

#386658 7 2007-12-05T21:35:40Z southpaw
About the depression:

This may only work for me, but I have a feeling that it could possibly work for a lot of people.

The only way I have found to overcome my depression is find something that connects to your childhood. It helps you think of simpler times. For me I watch "The Lion King" because that is my favorite Disney movie from when I was a kid. When I watch it I cry and get my depression out. The next day I start my "healing" process and within 24 hours of watching the movie I feel better. Once I am over being depressed I feel more productive, and I face things that I may have been avoiding.

A movie might not be the best thing for you. Possibly somewhere that you enjoyed being as a kid, something or somewhere or some person that you have fond memories of when you were little might be just the thing to help with depression. Once the depression is gone for the most part, one can start to work on things that need to be dealt with.


I hope that helps. If not you should ask others for help before looking into therapy, or some other form of professional help. It's cheaper to get advice from friends and family anyways
